--- title: "Basic Operations,
Basic Types of Data" author: "Enrico Toffalini" include-in-header: ../assets/slidesheader.html format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false css: custom.css theme: default slide-number: c/t self-contained: true code-fold: false code-summary: "Show code" code-overflow: wrap title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: "figures/psicostatLogo.png" data-background-size: "contain" data-background-opacity: "0.15" execute: echo: true output: true --- ## Create, name objects In R, **everything is an object**: variables, vectors, dataframes, functions, even entire environments. Let's create a variable named "`age`" that contains a single numerical value: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} age = 20 # assign number 20 to variable named "age" ``` ::: Now let's simply inspect its content: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} age ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # alternative way of showing content, # useful in programming when within functions or loops print(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # for more complex data structures the "str" function may be useful str(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` num 20 ``` ::: ::: ## Create, name objects ### Assignment operators In R, both the assignment operators "**`=`**" and "**`<-`**" (and actually even "**`->`**") can be used to assign values to objects. That said, "**`<-`**" is considered more traditional in R and often preferred for clarity, also because it allows differentiating assignment from other uses of "**`=`**". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # these two commands do the same thing age <- 20 age = 20 ``` ::: However, unlike many other teachers, I will generally favor "**`=`**" as the assignment operator in order to maintain consistency with the convention in most other programming languages. ## Create, name objects ### Rules for naming objects in R ***Strict rules:*** - Start with a letter or dot (if dot, must **not** be followed by a number); - Include only letters, numbers, dots, underscores; - No reserved words (e.g., `if`, `for`, `NA`, `function`; unless placed inside backticks, e.g., \`if\`, but this is strongly advised against). ***Recommendations:*** - Avoid names that conflict with common functions (e.g., "`mean`", "`sum`", "`c`"); - Be concise: no length limit, but long names are difficult to read and type. ⚠️ *WARNING!* R is case-sensitive: `age` and `Age` will be treated as **two objects**! ## Create, name objects ### Rules for naming objects in R *Examples:* - Allowed: "`age`", "`age0`", "`age1`", "`total_score`", "`.myData`", "`my.data`" - **NOT** allowed: "`0age`", "`_age`", "`.0myData`", "`my data`", "`my-data`", "`my,data`", "`for`", "`NA`" ⚠️ *WARNING!* The use of "`.`" in object names (e.g., "`my.data`") is fine in **R** but not allowed in **Python**, where "`.`" is part of the language syntax. Across different languages, *naming conventions* for longer, multi-word variable names favor **`snake_case`** (e.g., "`my_data`") or **`camelCase`** (e.g., "`myData`"), and **abbreviations** where appropriate (e.g., "`unipdData`" is better than "`university_of_padova_dataset`")... preferably used in a consistent way! ## Use basic operations ### R as calculator: some basic operators | Operator | What it does | Example | Result | |------------|-------------|------|------| | `+` | Addition| `5.4 + 6.1` |`11.5` | | `-` | Subtraction | `9 - 4.3` |`4.7` | | `*` | Multiplication | `7 * 1.4` |`9.8` | | `/` | Division| `9 / 12` |`0.75` | | `%/%` | Floor division| `13 %/% 4` |`3` | | `%%` | Modulus| `13 %% 4` |`1` | | `^` | Exponentiation| `15 ^ 2` |`225` | (also useful: object "`pi`" contains `3.1415927`) ## Use basic operations ### R as calculator: useful functions | Function | What it does | Example | Result | |---|--------|--------|------| | `abs` | absolute value | `abs(4.3-9.8)` |`5.5` | | `sqrt` | square root | `sqrt(176.4)` |`13.28157` | | `exp` | exponential function | `exp(2.2)` |`9.025013` ($e^{2.2}$) | | `log` | natural logarithm, base $e$ | `log(9.025013)` |`2.2` | | `log` | logarithm, given base | `log(10, base=2)` |`3.321928` | | `round` | round to integer | `round(1.7384)` |`2` | | `round` | round to digits | `round(1.7384, 2)` |`1.74` | ## Use basic operations ### R as calculator: use of parentheses The order of operations in R follows standard algebraic rules, unless you specify a different order using parentheses. In R, only round parentheses **`( )`** are used for grouping in algebraic expressions, **NOT** square **`[ ]`** or curly **`{ }`** brackets, because they have other specific syntactic purposes. *Examples:* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 2 * 3 + 3^2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 2 * (3 + 3)^2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 72 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} (2 * (3 + 3))^2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 144 ``` ::: ::: ## Use basic operations ### Relational operators They are used to compare values and return logical values (`TRUE`, `FALSE`). Let's say that we have defined `age = 20`; now let's look at a few examples: | Operator | What it does | Example | Result | |------------|-------------|------|------| | `==` | Equal to | `age == 18` |`FALSE` | | `!=` | Not equal to | `age != 18` |`TRUE` | | `>` | Greater than | `age > 18` |`TRUE` | | `<` | Less than | `age < 18` |`FALSE` | | `>=` | Greater than or equal to | `age >= 18` |`TRUE` | | `<=` | Less than or equal to | `age <= 18` |`FALSE` | ## Use basic operations ### Basic logical operators They are used to combine logical values (`TRUE`, `FALSE`). Once again, with `age = 20`, let's look at a few examples: | Operator | What it does | Example | Result | |------------|-------------|------|------| | `&` | AND | `age>25 & age<60` |`FALSE` | | `|` | OR | `age<25 | age>60` |`TRUE` | | `!` | NOT | `!(age<18)` |`TRUE` | 🙂 note that logical values are internally treated as integers: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} TRUE / 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.25 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 15 * FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Basic types of data ### numeric and logical So far, we have encountered at least two types of data: - **numeric** (`20`, `11.5`, `0`, `13.28157`, ...); - **logical/Boolean** (`TRUE`, `FALSE`). **Numeric** data can actually be of two types: ***double*** (i.e., "*double-precision floating-point*"), that is, with decimals like `11.5`, and ***integer***, like `20`. In fact, R treats numeric values as *double* by default (even if without decimals). To specify numbers as integers, explicitly add an **`L`** after the number, like `age = 20L` (you likely **will not** need this, unless you explicitly need integers for specific purposes, such as saving memory). ## Basic types of data ### strings / characters Another extremely important data type is **character** (most often called ***strings***). It is used to store text and must be enclosed in quotes (**`' '`** or **`" "`**) like this: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} myName = "Enrico" ``` ::: You may perform many operations with strings, like: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} myName == "Alexander" # is my name equal to Alexander? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} myName != "Alexander" # is my name NOT equal to Alexander? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} myName > "Alexander" # is my name larger than Alexander? (really?!) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ## Basic types of data ### basic working with strings: paste(), paste0(), and more **`paste()`** joins text with spaces, **`paste0()`** joins it without a separator. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paste("Hello", myName) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Hello Enrico" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} paste0("Fig", i, ".png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Fig1.png" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} nchar(myName) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} toupper(myName) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "ENRICO" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} With vectors, `paste0("subject_", 1:20)` will create participant labels as `"subject_1"`, `"subject_2"`, `"subject_3"`, `"subject_4"`, `"subject_5"`, ... ::: ## Basic types of data ### basic working with strings: find & replace **`gsub()`** replaces all matches in a string ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x = "12,5" as.numeric(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: NAs introduced by coercion ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ::: 🤔 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x = gsub(",", ".", x) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "12.5" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.numeric(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.5 ``` ::: ::: More examples: [Working with strings](../Examples-Tutorials/ExampleStrings.html){target="_blank"}. ## Basic types of data ### know the type of a variable The **`typeof()`** function tells you what type of data you are handling: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} myName = "Enrico" prof = TRUE coursesTaught = 4L age = 37 # see data types typeof(myName) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(prof) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(coursesTaught) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "double" ``` ::: ::: ## Basic types of data ### special values: `NA`, `NULL`, `NaN`, `Inf` **`NA`** is missing value of any type; **`NULL`** represents the absence of an object; **`NaN`** is an undefined numerical result; **`Inf`** is infinity. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 0/0 # NaN ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NaN ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 1/0 # Inf ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Inf ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.na(NA) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.nan(0/0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.null(NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: `is.na()` detects both `NA` and `NaN`; `is.nan()` specifically detects `NaN`. ## Basic types of data You may also check the data type directly with the `is.*` functions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} is.numeric(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.character(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.infinite(age/0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.logical(prof) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.integer(coursesTaught) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.integer(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.na(myName) # checks if a value is missing (i.e., NA) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
